newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW - Petrobras presence to grow outside Brazil.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Petrobras presence to grow outside Brazil.

text.p: The upcoming deregulation of Brazil's oil industry will not only bring new private investment to the sector but will also boost state oil giant Petrobras' operations outside of Brazil.

Petrobras has identified 150 projects to be carried out in joint ventures with private companies once the Brazilian Congress approves the petroleum bill, which regulates the opening of the oil sector to private capital.
The projects are mainly in exploration and production and are worth around $3 billion in investments over three years.

Jose Coutinho Barbosa, vice-president of Braspetro, a wholly-owned Petrobras subsidiary, told Reuters in a recent interview, the 68 companies interested in the partnership projects were almost all offering Petrobras business opportunities elsewhere in exchange.

Braspetro runs the oil giants' international exploration and production projects. Braspetro has been active in the world market for 25 years and currently operates in eight countries - Argentina, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, the United States, the United Kingdom, Libya, Angola.
"This is a way for Petrobras not to shrink in size but to exchange opportunities here for opportunities out there," Barbosa said. "These counter offers will no doubt increase the size of Braspetro."

He said it was too early to estimate how much the company could grow, but investment levels would increase at least 15 percent a year over the next five years, excluding the impact from the oil sector opening.
Braspetro is investing $350 million in its projects in 1997, up from $232 million last year.

The size of the Brazilian energy market will also boost Petrobras' presence abroad, especially in other Latin American countries which will give the company access to their oil and gas resources in exchange for market share in Brazil, he said.

This trend toward greater integration in Latin America's energy sector has been ongoing since the early 1990's when Petrobras started to import more oil from its neighbors at the expense of the Middle East, Barbosa said.

In 1996, 44 percent of Brazil's total crude oil imports came from Latin America as opposed to only four percent in 1990, and Argentina has become Brazil's biggest supplier with 143,000 bpd, followed by Saudi Arabia with 120,000 bpd and Venezuela with 82,000 bpd.
"Petrobras has played a major role in the integration of the Latin American energy market, something only few people have noticed," Barbosa said.

He said in coming years the biggest integration would take place in the natural gas sector because neighboring countries like Bolivia, Argentina, Peru and Venezuela had a lot of gas and Brazil had a gigantic market which was still growing.
Brazilian demand for natural gas, which currently accounts for two to three percent of Brazilian energy consumption, is expected to grow 20 percent a year over the next 10 years.

Potential economic demand for natural gas could grow from 40 million cubic meters per day in 1999 to nearly 80 million cubic meters per day in 2010 in Brazil's industrial heartland in the south, southeast and center of the country alone, according to a World Bank study.
In the north, northeast region of Brazil potential demand is expected to reach 40 million cubic meters per day by 2010.
Barbosa said once the $1.8 billion Bolivia-Brazil gas pipeline, under discussion for years, finally came online in late 1998 the Brazilian market would grow "tremendously".

The gas Braspetro has been exploring and producing together with Argentine oil and gas firm YPF SA in Argentina since 1993 and in Bolivia since last year will be sold in Brazil once the 1,900-mile pipeline is up and running.

While gas seems the most promising business opportunity for the future, Braspetro is also looking to continue integration in the oil sector by setting up a 50/50 joint venture with Venezuelan oil firm PDVSA.

"Venezuela will be producing a lot of oil and Brazil is a growing market," Barbosa said. "We don't just want to explore oil in Venezuela. We want to have a share in the profit from exploration, the profit from transportation, the profit from the sale of the product."

Braspetro and PDVSA officials are due to meet at the end of July to present possible projects in Venezuela and identify opportunities in the Brazilian market, but it is still to early to draw up a final shareholder agreement and determine investment in the new joint company, Petroamerica, Barbosa said.
((--Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151))
